query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains the mechanism expected to operate across the test regime, predicts performance relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, specifies relevant temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: A functionally graded, nanostructured surface coating deposited on a CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy can sustain a low friction coefficient and reduced wear rate across sliding tests from room temperature to 800 °C by promoting in situ formation of a protective, self-adaptive lubricious oxide (glaze) layer at high temperatures while remaining inert at lower temperatures.
generation.material_initial_state: CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy matrix exhibiting good tribological properties at room temperature but degrading (increased friction and wear) at elevated temperatures.
generation.intervention: Develop and deposit a functionally graded, nanostructured surface coating engineered to tailor oxidation kinetics so that at high temperatures (≥600 °C) it facilitates the formation of a stable lubricious oxide layer, whereas at room temperature it remains chemically and mechanically inert.
generation.conditions: Sliding tests conducted in an oxidizing environment (ambient air) over a temperature range from ~25 °C (room temperature) to 800 °C; applied normal loads ranging from low (≈5 N) to high (≈30 N) and sliding speeds between 1 and 5 mm/s.
generation.structural_mediator: The graded nanostructure that creates a compositional and microstructural interface, enabling controlled tribo-oxidation and optimized mechanical response across the temperature range.
generation.mechanism: At elevated temperatures, friction-induced heat triggers controlled oxidation in the engineered upper coating layers, forming a thin, continuous lubricious oxide glaze that minimizes adhesive and abrasive wear. At room temperature, the coating’s inert phase prevents premature oxidation, retaining the alloy’s original low-friction characteristics.
generation.predicted_outcome: The coated CoCrFeNi alloy will display consistently lower friction coefficients and reduced wear rates across the entire testing range compared to the unmodified alloy, especially improved performance at temperatures above 600 °C where the self-adaptive oxide glaze becomes active.
generation.baseline: The unmodified CoCrFeNi alloy, which maintains low friction and wear only at room temperature, but suffers degradation (higher friction and wear) as temperature increases.
generation.boundary: Performance is evaluated under sliding in ambient air with temperatures from ~25 °C to 800 °C, normal loads of approximately 5–30 N, and sliding speeds of 1–5 mm/s.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of performance improvement and long-term stability of the oxide glaze under cyclic thermal and mechanical stress remain to be quantified; optimization of the coating’s grading and composition is still required.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of unmodified CoCrFeNi alloys and another set with the functionally graded, nanostructured surface coating. Subject both sets to controlled sliding wear tests in ambient air across the temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C at identical normal loads (e.g., 30 N) and sliding speeds (e.g., 5 mm/s). Use in situ thermal imaging to monitor temperature evolution, and post-test analysis via SEM and EDS to characterize the presence and continuity of an oxide glaze, along with quantitative measurements of friction coefficients and wear scar dimensions.
measurements: Coefficient of friction over time at different temperatures
Wear rate (volume loss) and wear scar width
Microstructural characterization (via SEM) and chemical composition (via EDS) of the worn surfaces and any oxide glaze layers
Thermal imaging data to confirm local temperature profiles during sliding
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coated samples do not demonstrate a statistically significant reduction in friction coefficient and wear rate across the temperature range compared to the unmodified samples, or if the expected continuous and stable lubricious oxide layer does not form at high temperatures (≥600 °C), then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Thus, if cooperative heterostructures capable of releasing frictional stress in stages are configured in the alloy, it is expected to suppress the sliding-induced deformation. In contrast, upon wear at high temperatures (≥600 °C), the wear behavior of the material becomes quite complex, stemming from the prevalence of surface adhesion and tribo-oxidation at the friction interface [,]. High-temperature sliding tends to soften the metallic surface that endows the near-surface material susceptible to chemical instability caused by counterbody materials or environmental oxygen, triggering severe delamination wear and composition segregation at the friction interface that exacerbates wear [,]. Materials become more dependent on tribochemical protection upon high-temperature wear due to deterioration in stiffness [,]. Tribo-oxidation may promote the formation of a protective oxide layer (glaze layer) consisting of various nanocrystalline (NC) oxides on the worn surface, which assists in enhancing the friction interface while providing solid lubrication [,,]. If the worn surface is replaced by a glaze layer as tribo-oxidation accumulates, a gentle wear scenario can be achieved. Neverthele

Figure 13b presents a schematic diagram of the CoCrFeNiMo coating’s wear mechanism. During the sliding wear process, the high-speed friction between the Si3N4 ceramic ball and the HEA coating generated substantial frictional heating, gradually elevating the contact temperature. This thermal activation promoted the reaction between atmospheric oxygen and the elements in the HEA coating, resulting in the formation of a protective oxide layer. Wang et al. [], through Raman spectroscopy, found that the oxides were mainly composed of Fe3O4 and Fe2O3, with the presence of MoO3, NiO, Cr2O3, and Co3O4 as well. Among these, Fe3O4 and Fe2O3 played a positive role in the tribological properties of the HEA coating by reducing the coefficient of friction and enhancing frictional stability. However, prolonged testing induced progressive stress accumulation within the oxide layer, triggering adhesive wear at the tribo-interface. As the experiment advanced, cyclic shear stresses fragmented the oxide film into abrasive debris. Deprived of oxide protection, the hard σ-phase particles underwent brittle spallation during subsequent sliding, generating micron-scale pits that accelerated material loss.

frame.system: CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy matrix evaluated under sliding contact conditions. The baseline material shows acceptable tribological performance at room temperature but suffers from degradation (increased friction and wear) as temperature increases up to 800 °C.
frame.goal: Achieve consistently low coefficient of friction and minimal wear rate over the complete test range (room temperature to 800 °C) during sliding.
frame.limitation: The material’s tribological performance degrades over the wide temperature span, making it difficult to maintain low friction and wear simultaneously using the unmodified alloy.

frame.regime: Sliding contact tests performed from room temperature to 800 °C under controlled loads in an oxidizing environment (typical ambient or air conditions), which subject the material to both low and high temperature wear mechanisms.
prior_attempts: The starting CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy has been evaluated in its unmodified form, which exhibits good properties only in a limited temperature band. Previous approaches lacking a secondary phase or lubricating component have failed to sustain low friction and wear across the full temperature range.

decision.trend: Early studies on high-entropy alloy tribology began by incorporating a second phase (e.g. Y2O3 nanoparticles in PMC5706259) into the alloy matrix in order to strengthen the microstructure and improve wear resistance at room temperature. Later, researchers shifted toward designing nanohierarchical architectures (as in PMC10241162) that could activate adaptive friction interfaces, where controlled microstructural and compositional undulations promote the in‐situ formation of a lubricious glaze under sliding at high temperature. Although these efforts led to decreased wear and friction in parts of the temperature spectrum, none has yet offered a single, unified intervention that maintains optimal performance from room temperature up to 800 °C.
decision.unsolved: The critical challenge remains to sustain a low coefficient of friction and minimal wear rate continuously across this wide temperature range. Prior approaches either target improvements at lower temperatures (by strengthening the matrix via nanoparticle additions) or promote adaptive behavior at high temperatures (using nanostructured, compositionally undulated surfaces) but do not reconcile both regimes in a single intervention.
decision.lever: Develop and deposit a functionally graded, nanostructured surface coating on the CoCrFeNi matrix that is designed to promote an in situ, self-adaptive lubricious oxide/glaze layer during sliding at elevated temperatures while remaining inert at room temperature.
decision.why: This approach naturally follows from the observed trend of evolving from bulk dispersion techniques to adaptive, heterostructured surface designs. By engineering the surface/interfacial properties of the alloy, the coating can tailor the oxidation and reaction kinetics to provide low friction and wear protection across the entire temperature range, directly addressing the identified performance gap and meeting the design requirements.
